source: Speed-Time Graphs
On a speed-time graph a rising line means speeding up and a flat line means steady speed.
Students confuse a flat speed-time line (moving steadily) with a flat distance-time line (stopped).

A speed-time graph puts time along the bottom and speed up the side. It looks like a distance-time graph, but it tells a different story. Here the slope is the change in speed per second: the acceleration.
On a speed-time graph: a rising line means speeding up, a flat line means a steady speed, a falling line means slowing down, and a line along the time axis means stopped. Slope = acceleration.

Over any piece of the graph, the rise is a change in speed and the run is a time, so rise ÷ run is $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, the acceleration. A flat line has zero rise: the speed is not changing, but it is not zero either, so the object keeps moving.
The same motion on both graphs. While the speed graph is flat (2 s to 4 s), the distance graph is a straight rising line: steady speed, still moving.
A speed-time graph rises in a straight line from 2 m/s at 0 s to 14 m/s at 4 s. Find the acceleration.
Acceleration from the slope
$3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$
Slope: $a = \dfrac{12\,\mathrm{m/s}}{4\,\mathrm{s}} = 3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
A speed-time graph is flat at 8 m/s from 4 s to 10 s. What is happening, and how far does the object go?
A flat stretch
Steady speed; 48 m
Flat line: the speed stays 8 m/s, so the acceleration is 0.
The object is still moving: distance $= s\,t = 8\,\mathrm{m/s} \times 6\,\mathrm{s} = 48\,\mathrm{m}$.
That is the area of the rectangle under the line, 8 tall and 6 wide.

Mixing up the two graphs. A flat line on a distance-time graph means stopped. A flat line on a speed-time graph means moving at a steady speed. Check the label on the side axis before you read the shape.
Read the axis label first.
